seoTitle: Make an Instagram Grid Post in Canva Easily
metaDescription: Design a wide Instagram grid post in Canva and use the Image Splitter app, free on any plan, to slice it into tiles ready to post in order.
intro: A grid post is one wide image designed to split across several Instagram tiles, so it reads as a single banner when someone lands on your profile instead of a stack of unrelated squares. Instagram itself has no dedicated grid-post feature; this is a design convention built entirely on top of ordinary square posts and the order you upload them in. Canva makes the build approachable because the design work and the splitting happen in the same place: one wide canvas, then an app that slices it into individually exportable pieces. This guide walks through setting up that canvas, designing across it, and using Canva's Image Splitter to generate the files you'll upload to Instagram, in order.
costNote: Image Splitter is included on Canva's free plan. No Canva Pro subscription is required for this task.

steps.heading: Start a new wide canvas
steps.body: Open Canva and create a new design sized for a multi-tile layout, not a single square post: a wide canvas, several times the width of one Instagram tile, is what lets the splitter divide it evenly later. You land on a blank page with the full toolkit down the left side: Templates, Elements, Text, Uploads, and Tools. Because the canvas is intentionally oversized, zoom out first so you can see the whole thing while you design instead of working blind on a page that scrolls past the edges of your screen.

image.caption: A blank wide canvas set up ahead of designing, sized to be sliced into multiple tiles instead of posted as one image.

steps.heading: Design across the full width
steps.body: Treat the canvas as one continuous scene, not several separate posts glued together: text, graphics, and photos should flow across the width so the split doesn't cut through anything awkwardly. Drag in a background image, layer your headline and supporting text where they won't land on a tile seam, and use Canva's alignment guides to position things deliberately instead of eyeballing it. Sketch, mentally or literally, where each tile boundary will fall before you place text; a headline that straddles two tiles can look broken once it's split and posted as separate images.

image.caption: A finished wide design filling the canvas, the layout that will get sliced into individual grid tiles in the next step.

steps.heading: Open the Image Splitter app
steps.body: With the design finished, search Canva's Apps panel for Image Splitter and open it against your canvas. It's free on every Canva plan; no Pro subscription is required. The panel gives you control over file type (JPG is the standard choice for Instagram) along with size and quality sliders that determine how large and sharp each exported tile will be. Keep quality high unless file size is a real constraint: Instagram compresses the image again on upload, and starting from a soft export only compounds that loss.

image.caption: The Image Splitter panel, with file type set to JPG and sliders for export size and quality before generating the tiles.

steps.heading: Generate and review the split pieces
steps.body: Run the splitter and Canva adds new pages to your project, each a numbered slice of the original design: Split 1, Split 2, Split 3, and so on, in the order they'll need to be posted. A short processing step uploads the pieces to your media library automatically, and you can preview each page in the sidebar before exporting to confirm nothing got cut in an awkward spot. This is the moment to catch problems: if a face or a line of text got split across two tiles in a way that reads poorly, it's faster to fix now than after you've already scheduled the posts.

image.caption: Image Splitter generating the individual tiles as separate pages, each one ready to preview and export on its own.

steps.heading: Export each tile in the right order
steps.body: Download each split page individually, and label the files with a number prefix as you save them: 1-grid.jpg, 2-grid.jpg, and so on, so you don't lose track of the order once they're sitting in your camera roll or a shared folder. This step matters more than it sounds. Instagram grid posts only work if the tiles go up in the exact sequence they were split, and one out-of-order upload undoes the whole effect of the design.

steps.heading: Post the tiles in sequence
steps.body: Upload the pieces to Instagram back-to-back, in split order, close together in time so the grid reads as intentional and not a slow reveal. Some creators post right to left or bottom to top depending on how their grid is meant to be read, since Instagram profiles display posts in reverse-chronological order; plan your posting sequence around that before you start uploading, not after the first tile is already live.

troubleshooting.problem: Split tiles come out uneven sizes
troubleshooting.cause: The canvas width wasn't an exact multiple of the tile count you asked for.
troubleshooting.fix: Before opening Image Splitter, set canvas width to a clean multiple of one square tile's width, for example three times the tile width for a 3-tile row.

troubleshooting.problem: A face or line of text gets cut awkwardly across two tiles
troubleshooting.cause: The design was built without accounting for where each tile boundary falls.
troubleshooting.fix: Turn on alignment guides matching the tile width and rough in the split lines before placing the final artwork, not after.

faq.question: Do I need a Canva Pro subscription to split an image into a grid?
faq.answer: No. Image Splitter is available from Canva's Apps panel on every plan, including free.

faq.question: What size should my canvas be for a 3-tile grid post?
faq.answer: Set the canvas width to three times an Instagram tile's width at the same height, so the Image Splitter can divide it into three even, square-ish pieces.

faq.question: Why did my grid post look wrong after uploading?
faq.answer: The most common cause is posting the tiles out of order or with a delay between them. Instagram displays posts in reverse-chronological order, so plan your upload sequence to match how the design was split before you post the first tile.

faq.question: Can I use a photo instead of a graphic design for a grid post?
faq.answer: Yes. Upload a wide photo to your canvas, size the canvas to match its proportions, and run it through Image Splitter the same way you would a text-and-graphic design.

faq.question: Does a grid post help engagement?
faq.answer: A cohesive, deliberately designed grid tends to make a profile look more polished at a glance, which can encourage a new visitor to keep scrolling and follow, though results vary by audience and content type.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from the original recording. Canva doesn't publish a dedicated help-center walkthrough for the Image Splitter app, and Instagram has no official documentation for the grid-post convention itself since it isn't a native Instagram layout. Verification here is limited to what could be checked: Image Splitter's free-plan availability, confirmed against Canva's own Image Splitter app listing in September 2026, which is what corrected the earlier hedge about possibly needing Canva Pro.
